lessons.title: Forces, Mass and Weight
lessons.description: What forces do, how they pair up, and why mass and weight are fundamentally different things.
lessons.content_html:
What Is a Force?

A force is a push or a pull that acts on an object. Forces can change the shape of an object, change its speed, or change the direction it is moving. They are measured in newtons (N) and are vector quantities — meaning both their size and direction must be stated.

Forces come in two categories. Contact forces require the objects to be touching — examples include friction, air resistance, tension in a rope, and the normal contact force (the push a surface exerts on an object resting on it). Non-contact forces act at a distance without the objects touching — examples include gravity, magnetic forces and electrostatic forces.

Key Fact

Contact forces (friction, tension, normal contact, air resistance) require physical contact. Non-contact forces (gravity, magnetism, electrostatics) act at a distance without touching. Forces are vectors — they have both size and direction.

Mass and Weight

Mass and weight are different quantities that students frequently confuse. Mass is the amount of matter in an object. It is a scalar quantity (magnitude only, no direction), measured in kilograms (kg), and it does not change wherever you go in the universe.

Weight is the gravitational force acting on an object’s mass. It is a vector quantity, measured in newtons (N), and it depends on where you are. The same astronaut has the same mass on Earth and on the Moon, but a much smaller weight on the Moon because the Moon’s gravitational field strength is much weaker.

The relationship between mass, weight and gravitational field strength is:

$$W = m \times g$$

Where \(W\) is weight (N), \(m\) is mass (kg), and \(g\) is gravitational field strength (N/kg). On Earth’s surface, \(g = 10 \text{ N/kg}\) (or 9.8 N/kg to two significant figures). Weight is measured using a newton meter (spring balance) and always acts downwards towards the centre of the attracting body.

Question: A student has a mass of 60 kg. Calculate their weight on Earth (\(g = 10 \text{ N/kg}\)) and on the Moon (\(g = 1.6 \text{ N/kg}\)).

On Earth: \(W = m \times g = 60 \times 10 = 600 \text{ N}\).
On the Moon: \(W = 60 \times 1.6 = 96 \text{ N}\).
Notice: mass stays at 60 kg in both cases. Only weight changes because \(g\) changes.

Free-Body Diagrams

A free-body diagram shows all the forces acting on a single object as arrows. The length of each arrow represents the magnitude of the force; the direction of the arrow shows where the force acts. By convention, forces are drawn acting from the centre of the object outwards in the direction they act.

A book resting on a table has two forces acting on it: its weight (downwards, caused by gravity) and the normal contact force from the table (upwards, caused by the table pushing back on the book). When these two forces are equal in size and opposite in direction, the book is in equilibrium — it does not accelerate.

When forces acting on an object are balanced (the resultant force is zero), the object either remains at rest or continues at constant velocity. When forces are unbalanced, the resultant force causes acceleration in the direction of the larger force. This is the foundation of Newton’s First Law.

Key Fact

In a free-body diagram, balanced forces (equal size, opposite direction) mean zero resultant force and no acceleration. Unbalanced forces produce acceleration. Arrows show direction; length shows magnitude.

Resultant Forces

The resultant force is the overall effect of all forces combined. For forces acting along the same line, you simply add or subtract them. For example, if a car engine produces a forward force of 2000 N and friction produces a backward force of 800 N, the resultant force is 1200 N forwards — the car accelerates.

When forces act at an angle to each other, you use a scale drawing (or Pythagoras’s theorem for right angles) to find the resultant. Resolving forces into components is a Higher-tier skill, but understanding that the resultant is the “net” force is essential at all levels.

Newton’s Third Law states: when object A exerts a force on object B, object B exerts an equal and opposite force on object A. These are called a Newton’s Third Law pair. They are always equal in size, opposite in direction, the same type of force, and act on different objects.

For example, when a person stands on the ground, the Earth pulls the person downwards (weight) and the person pulls the Earth upwards with an equal gravitational force. Separately, the ground pushes the person upwards (normal contact force) and the person pushes the ground downwards with an equal contact force. These are two distinct force pairs. A common error is treating weight and normal contact force as a Newton’s Third Law pair — they are not, because they act on the same object (the person).
lessons.exam_tip_html: The mass vs weight distinction is a reliable mark in every paper. Always state that mass is in kg (a scalar) and weight is in N (a vector force caused by gravity). In free-body diagram questions, check whether forces are balanced or unbalanced before deciding if there is acceleration. For Newton’s Third Law questions, confirm that paired forces act on different objects — if they act on the same object they cannot be a Third Law pair.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Forces are vectors (size + direction). Contact forces require touching (friction, tension, normal); non-contact forces act at a distance (gravity, magnetism, electrostatics).
  • Mass (kg) is the amount of matter and does not change location. Weight (N) = m × g; it depends on gravitational field strength and acts downwards.
  • Free-body diagrams show all forces on one object. Balanced forces mean zero resultant force and no acceleration. The resultant force is the net combined effect of all forces.

Friction and air resistance together produce a backward force of 200 N. Calculate the resultant force on the cyclist and bicycle system, then suggest what would happen to their motion.
practice_questions.marks:
Developing: Identifies that resultant force = 500 − 200 = 300 N forwards (1 mark).
Secure: States that because there is an unbalanced resultant force, the system will accelerate (1 mark).
Mastering: Calculates acceleration using F = ma: total mass = 70 + 15 = 85 kg; a = 300/85 ≈ 3.5 m/s² (1 mark). Suggests the cyclist continues to speed up until air resistance increases enough to balance the engine force (terminal velocity) (1 mark). [4 marks]

practice_questions.marks:
Developing: Identifies that Newton’s Third Law pairs act on different objects.
Secure: Correctly identifies the Third Law pair for weight: the book pulls the Earth upwards with a gravitational force equal and opposite to its weight (1 mark). This force acts on the Earth, not the book (1 mark).
Mastering: Explains that weight and normal contact force are NOT a Third Law pair because they both act on the same object (the book) (1 mark); also, they are different types of force — weight is gravitational, normal contact force is mechanical — whereas Third Law pairs must be the same type of force (1 mark). [4 marks]

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the importance of correctly distinguishing between mass and weight in real-world scientific contexts. Use at least two specific examples in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Emerging: States that mass and weight are different and have different units.
Developing: Explains that mass is constant everywhere (kg) and weight depends on gravitational field strength (N) using W = mg (1 mark). Gives one relevant example, such as space engineering (1 mark).
Secure: Provides two specific examples, e.g. (1) spacecraft design — engineers must account for the different weight of the craft on different planets even though mass is unchanged (1 mark); (2) medical measurement — clinical drug doses are calculated by mass (kg) not weight, because mass is constant regardless of where the patient is measured (1 mark).
Mastering: Evaluates the consequences of confusing the two — e.g. a spacecraft calibrated for Earth weight but used on Mars would have incorrect thrust calculations; a drug dose based on weight in newtons would vary by location and could cause harm. Reaches a reasoned conclusion about why the distinction matters scientifically and practically (2 further marks). [6 marks — levels marked]

lessons.title: Describing Motion
lessons.description: Speed, velocity, acceleration, and how to read distance-time and velocity-time graphs.
lessons.content_html:
Speed and Velocity

Speed tells you how fast an object moves, but not which direction. It is a scalar quantity — it has magnitude but no direction. The equation is:

$$s = v \times t$$

Where \(s\) is distance (m), \(v\) is speed (m/s), and \(t\) is time (s). Rearranged: \(v = \frac{s}{t}\) or \(t = \frac{s}{v}\). Typical speeds to be familiar with: walking ~1.5 m/s, running ~3 m/s, cycling ~6 m/s, a car in a town ~13 m/s, and the speed of sound in air ~340 m/s.

Velocity is speed in a stated direction. It is a vector quantity. An object travelling around a circular track at constant speed has a changing velocity, because direction is continuously changing — so it is always accelerating.

Distance (scalar) measures the total path length travelled. Displacement (vector) measures how far — and in what direction — an object is from its starting point. A runner who completes one full lap of a 400 m track has covered a distance of 400 m but has a displacement of zero.

Key Fact

Scalars have magnitude only: speed, distance, mass, energy. Vectors have magnitude AND direction: velocity, displacement, force, acceleration. An object moving in a circle has a constantly changing velocity (direction changes) even if speed is constant.

Acceleration

Acceleration is how quickly velocity changes. It can mean speeding up, slowing down (deceleration), or changing direction. The equation is:

$$a = \frac{v - u}{t}$$

Where \(a\) is acceleration (m/s2), \(v\) is final velocity (m/s), \(u\) is initial velocity (m/s), and \(t\) is time (s). A negative acceleration (deceleration) means the object is slowing down. For example, a car braking from 20 m/s to rest in 4 s has \(a = \frac{0 - 20}{4} = -5 \text{ m/s}^2\).

Question: A cyclist accelerates from 4 m/s to 12 m/s in 5 seconds. Calculate the acceleration.

Answer: \(a = \frac{v - u}{t} = \frac{12 - 4}{5} = \frac{8}{5} = 1.6 \text{ m/s}^2\). The cyclist is accelerating at 1.6 m/s2 in the direction of travel.

Distance-Time Graphs

On a distance-time graph, the gradient (slope) of the line equals the speed. Interpreting the shapes:

• Horizontal line — the object is stationary (speed = 0).
• Straight diagonal line — constant speed; steeper gradient means faster.
• Curve getting steeper — the object is accelerating.
• Curve getting shallower — the object is decelerating.

To find speed at a specific moment on a curved distance-time graph, draw a tangent to the curve at that point and calculate the gradient of the tangent. The tangent is a straight line that just touches the curve at one point and has the same slope as the curve there.

Key Fact

On a distance-time graph: gradient = speed. Horizontal = stopped. Straight line = constant speed. Curve getting steeper = accelerating. To find instantaneous speed on a curve, draw a tangent and calculate its gradient.

Velocity-Time Graphs

On a velocity-time graph, two pieces of information can be extracted:

• The gradient equals the acceleration. Steep upward slope = large acceleration. Horizontal line = constant velocity (zero acceleration). Downward slope = deceleration.
• A line below the x-axis means the object is moving in the opposite direction to the positive direction defined in the question.

The area under the line on a velocity-time graph equals the distance travelled. For a triangular shape: area = \(\frac{1}{2} \times \text{base} \times \text{height}\). For a rectangular shape: area = base × height. Complex shapes are split into triangles and rectangles and summed.

Scenario: A train accelerates from 0 to 30 m/s in 10 s, then travels at constant 30 m/s for 20 s, then decelerates to rest in 5 s.

Acceleration phase: gradient = \(\frac{30 - 0}{10} = 3 \text{ m/s}^2\).
Constant phase: gradient = 0, so acceleration = 0 m/s2, constant velocity.
Deceleration phase: gradient = \(\frac{0 - 30}{5} = -6 \text{ m/s}^2\) (deceleration of 6 m/s2).

Uniform and Non-Uniform Acceleration

Uniform (constant) acceleration produces a straight line on a velocity-time graph. Non-uniform acceleration (changing acceleration) produces a curve. For uniform acceleration, you can also use:

$$v^2 = u^2 + 2as$$

Where \(s\) is distance (m). This equation is useful when time is not given — for example, calculating braking distance given initial speed and deceleration. Real-world journeys almost always involve non-uniform acceleration — average speed is found by dividing total distance by total time.

Motion and Road Safety

The physics of motion has direct consequences for road safety. Stopping distance is the total distance a vehicle travels from when a driver notices a hazard to when the vehicle comes to rest. It has two parts:

• Thinking distance — the distance covered at constant speed during the driver’s reaction time (typically 0.2–0.9 s depending on alertness). Increased by tiredness, alcohol, or drug use.
• Braking distance — the distance covered while decelerating to rest. Increased by higher speed (because kinetic energy \(E_k = \frac{1}{2}mv^2\) grows with the square of speed), wet or icy roads (reduced friction), or worn tyres and brakes.

Because braking distance scales with \(v^2\), doubling speed more than doubles stopping distance. A car travelling at 30 mph on a dry road requires roughly 23 m to stop; at 60 mph, the stopping distance is approximately 73 m — more than three times greater for twice the speed. This is why speed limits in residential areas are low — the consequences of a collision at lower speed are far less severe.
lessons.exam_tip_html: The most common mistake on graph questions is confusing a steep section with a large value. On a distance-time graph, steep means fast; on a velocity-time graph, steep means large acceleration, not large speed. Always state what the gradient or area represents before calculating it. For ‘Suggest’ questions about motion, identify the relevant equation (distance-speed-time or acceleration equation) and apply it to the novel scenario given.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Speed (m/s) is scalar. Velocity (m/s + direction) is vector. Acceleration (m/s2) = change in velocity ÷ time. All three link via the equations s = vt and a = (v - u)/t.
  • Distance-time graph: gradient = speed. Horizontal = stopped, straight line = constant speed, curve = changing speed.
  • Velocity-time graph: gradient = acceleration. Horizontal = constant velocity. Stopping distance = thinking distance + braking distance; both increase with speed.

practice_questions.text: Speed cameras monitor road safety. Evaluate how the physics of motion can be used to determine whether a driver was speeding and whether they were driving safely, beyond just measuring speed.
practice_questions.marks:
Emerging: States that speed cameras measure speed using distance and time.

Mastering: Evaluates the limitations — speed cameras capture a snapshot in time and may miss dangerous accelerations or tailgating; physics suggests that speed alone is insufficient — safe driving depends on speed relative to conditions (road surface, visibility, traffic) (1 mark). Reaches a reasoned conclusion about what additional data (e.g. acceleration profiles, inter-vehicle distance) would give a fuller picture of safety (1 mark). [6 marks — levels marked]

lessons.title: Forces, Acceleration and Stopping
lessons.description: Newton's laws, F = ma, momentum, and why braking distance grows quickly with speed.
lessons.content_html:
Newton's First Law

Newton's First Law states that an object remains at rest, or continues to move at a constant velocity, unless a resultant force acts on it. A resultant force is the single force that represents the combined effect of all forces acting on an object.

If the resultant force is zero, a stationary object stays still and a moving object keeps moving at the same speed in the same direction. If there is a resultant force, the object accelerates — meaning it speeds up, slows down, or changes direction. A spacecraft drifting in deep space, where there is no friction or air resistance, will continue at the same velocity indefinitely unless a thruster fires. This is not because a force is pushing it — it is because no force is acting to slow it down.

Key Fact

Objects do not need a force to keep moving at constant velocity. A resultant force is only needed to change the speed or direction of an object — this is a very common exam misconception.

Newton's Second Law: F = ma

Newton's Second Law tells us that the resultant force on an object equals its mass multiplied by its acceleration:

$$F = m \times a$$

Where \(F\) is force in newtons (N), \(m\) is mass in kilograms (kg), and \(a\) is acceleration in m/s². A bigger force produces a bigger acceleration (if mass stays the same), and a heavier object needs a bigger force for the same acceleration. The equation rearranges to \(a = \frac{F}{m}\) or \(m = \frac{F}{a}\). Always use the resultant force, not any single force in isolation. If a car engine provides 3 000 N but friction and air resistance total 1 000 N, the resultant force is 2 000 N forward.

Question: A 1 200 kg car experiences a resultant force of 3 600 N. Calculate its acceleration.

Step 1: Write the equation: \(a = \frac{F}{m}\)

Step 2: Substitute: \(a = \frac{3600}{1200} = 3 \text{ m/s}^2\)

Now try: A 0.5 kg ball is kicked with a resultant force of 35 N. What is its acceleration? (Answer: 70 m/s²)

Newton's Third Law

Newton's Third Law states: for every action force there is an equal and opposite reaction force. These forces always act on different objects and are always the same type of force. When a swimmer pushes water backwards, the water pushes the swimmer forwards with an equal force. When a rocket expels gases downwards, the gases push the rocket upwards with an equal force.

A common mistake is to confuse a Third Law pair with balanced forces. Balanced forces act on the same object. A Third Law pair always involves forces on different objects. Weight (Earth pulling you down) and normal contact force (ground pushing you up) are NOT a Third Law pair — both act on you. The Third Law pair of your weight is the gravitational pull you exert on the Earth.

Key Fact

Newton's Third Law pairs are always equal in size, opposite in direction, the same type of force, and act on different objects from each other.

Momentum

Momentum is the product of an object's mass and velocity:

$$p = m \times v$$

Where \(p\) is momentum in kg m/s, \(m\) is mass in kg, and \(v\) is velocity in m/s. In a closed system (no external forces), the total momentum before an event equals the total momentum after — this is the conservation of momentum. If a 2 kg trolley moving at 4 m/s collides with and sticks to a stationary 2 kg trolley, momentum before = \(2 \times 4 = 8\) kg m/s. After, the combined 4 kg mass moves at \(\frac{8}{4} = 2\) m/s. Momentum is conserved; kinetic energy is not.

Stopping distance is the sum of two parts:

• Thinking distance — the distance travelled during the driver's reaction time (between seeing the hazard and pressing the brake). Factors that increase thinking distance: tiredness, alcohol, drugs, distractions, higher speed.
• Braking distance — the distance travelled after the brakes are applied. Factors that increase braking distance: higher speed, wet or icy roads, worn tyres, worn or overheated brakes.

Speed has a particularly large effect on braking distance because kinetic energy depends on \(v^2\). Doubling speed quadruples kinetic energy, so the brakes must do four times more work to stop the vehicle — meaning roughly four times the braking distance. This is why motorway speed limits are strictly enforced.

Large braking forces are needed to stop quickly. A very large braking force causes the tyres to skid, reducing control. Modern vehicles use anti-lock braking systems (ABS) to prevent skidding by modulating brake pressure automatically.

Key Fact

Stopping distance = thinking distance + braking distance. Braking distance is proportional to \(v^2\) — doubling speed roughly quadruples braking distance. Speed is the most significant factor in serious collisions.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For a 3-mark explain question on stopping distance, structure your answer using causal language: 'At higher speeds, the car has greater kinetic energy, so the brakes must do more work to stop it, meaning the braking distance is longer.' For a 4-mark compare/suggest on Newton's laws, always state which law you are applying before explaining it. For 6-mark extended responses on momentum or road safety, evaluate the risk factors — don't just list them. Use the StudyVault Mastering rubric: state the science, apply it to the context, and evaluate the consequence.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Newton's First Law: objects keep their velocity unless a resultant force acts. Objects do not need a force to keep moving.
  • Newton's Second Law: \(F = ma\). Always use the resultant force. Rearrange to find acceleration or mass as needed.
  • Newton's Third Law: every action has an equal and opposite reaction on a different object.
  • Momentum \(p = mv\) is conserved in closed systems. Stopping distance = thinking distance + braking distance, and braking distance grows with speed squared.

lessons.title: Energy Stores, Transfers and Work
lessons.description: Energy stores, conservation, work done, kinetic and gravitational potential energy.
lessons.content_html:
Energy Stores and Conservation

The law of conservation of energy is one of the most fundamental principles in physics: energy cannot be created or destroyed — only transferred between stores. In any closed system, the total energy before a process equals the total energy after. Energy that appears to 'disappear' has been dissipated — spread out into thermal energy in the surroundings where it cannot easily be recovered.

There are eight main energy stores: kinetic (moving objects), gravitational potential (objects at height), elastic potential (stretched or compressed materials), chemical (food, fuels, batteries), thermal (hot objects), magnetic, electrostatic and nuclear. Energy transfers between stores via four pathways: heating, radiation, electrical working, and mechanical working.

Key Fact

Energy cannot be created or destroyed. It transfers between stores (kinetic, gravitational potential, elastic, chemical, thermal, and others). Any energy that is 'wasted' is dissipated as thermal energy in the surroundings.

Work Done

When a force moves an object through a distance, work is done. Work done equals the energy transferred. The equation is:

$$W = F \times d$$

Where \(W\) is work done in joules (J), \(F\) is force in newtons (N), and \(d\) is distance moved in the direction of the force in metres (m). One joule of work is done when a force of 1 N moves an object 1 m. Work done and energy transferred are equivalent — both are measured in joules.

Example: a person pushes a shopping trolley with 40 N of force across 5 m. Work done = \(40 \times 5 = 200\) J. This energy is transferred from the person's chemical energy store into the kinetic energy of the trolley (and some to thermal energy through friction with the floor).

Question: A builder lifts bricks weighing 600 N to a scaffold 4 m above the ground. How much work is done?

Step 1: Identify equation: \(W = F \times d\)

Step 2: Substitute: \(W = 600 \times 4 = 2400 \text{ J}\)

Interpretation: This 2 400 J has been transferred from the builder's chemical energy store into the gravitational potential energy store of the bricks.

Kinetic and Gravitational Potential Energy

A moving object stores kinetic energy (KE):

$$KE = \frac{1}{2} \times m \times v^2$$

Where \(m\) is mass in kg and \(v\) is speed in m/s. Notice that KE depends on \(v^2\) — doubling speed quadruples kinetic energy. This is why road speed limits have such a large effect on collision severity.

An object at height stores gravitational potential energy (GPE):

$$GPE = m \times g \times h$$

Where \(m\) is mass (kg), \(g\) is gravitational field strength (10 N/kg on Earth's surface), and \(h\) is height (m). A 3 kg book placed on a shelf 1.5 m high gains GPE = \(3 \times 10 \times 1.5 = 45\) J relative to the floor.

When an object falls freely (ignoring air resistance), GPE converts into KE. At the start all energy is stored as GPE; at the bottom all has converted to KE. At any point in between, total energy = GPE + KE = constant. This allows you to calculate the speed of a falling object using \(GPE_{lost} = KE_{gained}\), i.e. \(mgh = \frac{1}{2}mv^2\). The masses cancel, giving \(v = \sqrt{2gh}\).

Example: A ball dropped from 5 m above the ground (ignoring air resistance): \(v = \sqrt{2 \times 10 \times 5} = \sqrt{100} = 10 \text{ m/s}\) just before hitting the ground. In reality, air resistance dissipates some energy as thermal energy in the air, so the actual speed would be slightly less.

Efficiency

No device transfers energy with 100% efficiency — some is always dissipated as wasted thermal energy. Efficiency is calculated as:

$$\text{Efficiency} = \frac{\text{useful output energy}}{\text{total input energy}}$$

Efficiency can be expressed as a decimal (0 to 1) or multiplied by 100 to give a percentage. A motor that receives 400 J of electrical energy and performs 280 J of useful work has efficiency = \(\frac{280}{400} = 0.70\) = 70%. The remaining 120 J is wasted as heat and sound. Engineers improve efficiency through lubrication (reducing friction), streamlining (reducing air resistance) and thermal insulation.

Key Fact

Efficiency = useful output energy ÷ total input energy. No device is 100% efficient. KE = ½mv² and GPE = mgh are the two key energy store equations — both appear regularly in exam calculations.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For calculation questions involving KE = ½mv², remember the v is squared — a very common error is to forget to square the velocity. Always show your working clearly: write the equation, substitute values with units, then evaluate. For 4-mark compare/suggest questions on energy transfers, name the energy stores at the start and end and describe the pathway (e.g. 'mechanical working'). For 6-mark extended responses on efficiency and energy, evaluate whether the energy loss is acceptable given the context — this is the levels-mark difference between Secure and Mastering.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Energy is conserved — it transfers between stores but is never created or destroyed. Dissipated energy is thermal energy in the surroundings.
  • Work done = force × distance (\(W = Fd\)), measured in joules. Work done equals energy transferred.
  • Kinetic energy: \(KE = \frac{1}{2}mv^2\). Doubling speed quadruples KE. Gravitational potential energy: \(GPE = mgh\).
  • Efficiency = useful output ÷ total input. Engineers reduce waste through lubrication, streamlining and insulation.

lessons.title: Radioactivity: Atoms and Nuclear Decay
lessons.description: Isotopes, alpha, beta and gamma decay, half-life and nuclear equations.
lessons.content_html:
Atomic Structure and Isotopes

Every atom has a nucleus made of protons (positive charge) and neutrons (no charge). Electrons (negative charge) occupy energy levels around the nucleus. The number of protons defines the element — carbon always has 6 protons, oxygen always has 8. In a neutral atom, the number of electrons equals the number of protons.

Isotopes are atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons. They have the same atomic number (protons) but different mass numbers (protons + neutrons). We write isotopes in nuclear notation: \(^A_Z X\) where \(A\) is the mass number and \(Z\) is the atomic number. For example, carbon-12 (\(^{12}_{6}\text{C}\)) has 6 protons and 6 neutrons, while carbon-14 (\(^{14}_{6}\text{C}\)) has 6 protons and 8 neutrons. Some isotopes have unstable nuclei that emit radiation spontaneously — these are radioactive isotopes.

Key Fact

Isotopes have the same atomic number (protons) but different mass numbers (protons + neutrons). Radioactive decay is a random, spontaneous process — individual decay events cannot be predicted.

Types of Radiation

Unstable nuclei emit three main types of radiation, each with different properties:

• Alpha (α) particles — 2 protons + 2 neutrons (equivalent to a helium-4 nucleus, \(^4_2\text{He}\)). Strongly ionising because of their large charge and mass. Weakly penetrating: stopped by a sheet of paper, a few centimetres of air, or skin.
• Beta (β) particles — a high-speed electron emitted when a neutron converts into a proton inside the nucleus. Moderately ionising and moderately penetrating: stopped by a few millimetres of aluminium.
• Gamma (γ) rays — electromagnetic radiation emitted when the nucleus releases excess energy. Weakly ionising but highly penetrating: only significantly reduced by thick lead or several metres of concrete. Often emitted alongside alpha or beta decay.

In nuclear equations, both mass numbers and atomic numbers must balance on each side of the arrow.

Alpha decay: the nucleus loses 2 protons and 2 neutrons. Mass number decreases by 4, atomic number decreases by 2. Example — uranium-238 decays to thorium-234:

$$^{238}_{92}\text{U} \rightarrow ^{234}_{90}\text{Th} + ^{4}_{2}\text{He}$$

Beta decay: a neutron converts to a proton, emitting an electron from the nucleus. Mass number stays the same, atomic number increases by 1. Example — carbon-14 decays to nitrogen-14:

$$^{14}_{6}\text{C} \rightarrow ^{14}_{7}\text{N} + ^{0}_{-1}\text{e}$$

Gamma emission: the nucleus releases excess energy as a gamma ray. No change to mass number or atomic number — it is not shown as a separate particle in the equation.

Key Fact

Alpha: −4 mass, −2 atomic. Beta: same mass, +1 atomic. Gamma: no change. Both mass numbers and atomic numbers must balance in every nuclear equation.

Ionisation and Detecting Radiation

Ionisation occurs when radiation knocks electrons from atoms, creating charged ions. Alpha particles are the most ionising — they transfer their energy quickly because of their large charge and mass. Gamma rays are the least ionising but travel the furthest. Ionisation in living cells can damage DNA, potentially causing mutations or cancer. The greater the ionising power, the lower the penetrating power — alpha radiation is stopped quickly because it transfers its energy so readily.

The activity of a radioactive source is measured in becquerels (Bq), where 1 Bq = 1 decay per second. In the laboratory, a Geiger–Müller (GM) tube detects ionising radiation and records a count rate in counts per second or per minute. When measuring a source, always account for background radiation — the low-level radiation always present in the environment from natural sources (radon gas, cosmic rays, food and building materials) and, to a much smaller extent, artificial sources.

Half-Life

Half-life is the time taken for half of the unstable nuclei in a sample to decay — equivalently, the time for the activity to halve. Radioactive decay is random: we cannot predict when any individual nucleus will decay, but statistical behaviour of large numbers of nuclei is reliable and predictable.

After one half-life, half the original unstable nuclei remain. After two half-lives, a quarter remain. After three, an eighth. For example, if a sample has an activity of 800 Bq and its half-life is 3 hours, after 9 hours (3 half-lives): \(800 \rightarrow 400 \rightarrow 200 \rightarrow 100\) Bq.

On a graph of activity against time, the curve falls steeply at first and then more gradually — this is an exponential decay curve. To read the half-life from the graph: identify the starting activity, find the time at which it has halved, and read across. Then check: does the activity halve again in the same time interval? It should — half-life is constant for a given isotope regardless of how much of the material is left.

In the laboratory, plotting count rate against time (after subtracting background count rate) gives the same exponential shape. The corrected count rate should be used — not the raw reading — to ensure you are measuring only the decay of the source.

Key Fact

Half-life is the time for activity (or number of unstable nuclei) to halve. It is constant for a given isotope. Radioactive decay cannot be sped up or slowed down by changing physical conditions such as temperature or pressure.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For nuclear equation questions, write the equation and then check: do mass numbers balance? Do atomic numbers balance? Missing particles can be found by subtraction. For half-life questions, use the step-by-step repeated-halving method rather than trying to use a formula — it is less error-prone and shows your working clearly. For 6-mark extended responses on radioactivity, always connect properties of the radiation (ionising power, penetrating power) to the application or risk being discussed — this is what earns levels-mark credit.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Isotopes are atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons. Radioactive isotopes have unstable nuclei that decay spontaneously and randomly.
  • Alpha (α): 2 protons + 2 neutrons, most ionising, least penetrating. Beta (β): fast electron, moderate. Gamma (γ): electromagnetic, least ionising, most penetrating.
  • In decay equations, both mass number and atomic number must balance. Alpha: −4 mass, −2 atomic. Beta: +1 atomic, same mass.
  • Half-life is the time for activity to halve. It is constant for a given isotope and cannot be changed by external conditions.

To improve confidence: repeat the experiment several times and calculate a mean; use longer measurement periods for each reading to smooth out random variations; ensure background radiation has been correctly subtracted each time. lessons.title: Using Radioactive Materials Safely
lessons.description: Contamination vs irradiation, medical uses of radioisotopes, and managing nuclear waste.
lessons.content_html:
Contamination and Irradiation

It is essential to distinguish between two ways a person can be exposed to radiation:

Contamination — a radioactive material is deposited on or inside the body. The person effectively carries a radiation source with them; the exposure is continuous and cannot be stopped simply by moving away. Contamination is removed by washing or specialist decontamination procedures. Even weakly penetrating radiation such as alpha particles becomes highly dangerous when the source is inside the body, because it ionises tissue directly.

Irradiation — the person is exposed to radiation from an external source but does not take the radioactive material into their body. They do not become radioactive. The exposure stops as soon as they move away from the source. The risk from irradiation depends on the type of radiation, the dose received and the duration of exposure.

Key Fact

Contamination = radioactive material inside or on the body — ongoing risk. Irradiation = external exposure — stops when the source is removed. Contamination is generally considered more dangerous because it provides continuous exposure.

Medical Uses of Radioactive Materials

Radioactive materials have several well-established medical uses. The choice of isotope depends on the type of radiation emitted, its half-life and its toxicity to the body:

• Medical tracers: a patient swallows or is injected with a radioactive tracer. The tracer uses a gamma-emitting isotope with a short half-life — gamma rays penetrate the body and are detected externally by a scanner. This lets doctors diagnose conditions such as cancer, blocked arteries or kidney problems without surgery. The short half-life ensures the patient's radiation exposure is minimised once the procedure is complete.
• PET scans: positron emission tomography uses a short-lived radioactive tracer that emits positrons (\(\beta^+\) particles). These annihilate with electrons in the body, producing pairs of gamma rays that are detected simultaneously. PET scans are used to detect metabolically active tumours and to image brain activity.
• Radiotherapy: high doses of gamma rays or beta particles are targeted at tumours to kill the rapidly dividing cancer cells. Multiple beams from different angles converge on the tumour, so healthy tissue receives a lower dose from each individual beam while the tumour receives the full combined dose.

For a medical tracer, a gamma emitter is used because gamma rays can penetrate the body and be detected externally — alpha or beta particles would not reach the detector. A short half-life (typically a few hours) is preferred: long enough to complete the scan, short enough to minimise the patient's total radiation dose. Once imaging is complete, the activity drops rapidly.

For industrial thickness gauging (such as controlling the thickness of metal sheets or paper during manufacture), beta emitters with longer half-lives are used. The source needs to last for months or years in service without requiring frequent replacement. Too little radiation passes through if the material is too thick; too much if it is too thin — automated systems adjust rollers accordingly.

For cancer radiotherapy, high-energy gamma sources or carefully aimed beams of radiation are used. The treatment must be planned precisely using imaging data so that the radiation dose to healthy tissue is minimised while the tumour receives a lethal dose.

Risk–Benefit Reasoning (IaS4)

Decisions about using radioactive materials always involve weighing evidence about benefits against evidence about risks. This kind of reasoning — considering both sides under uncertainty — is central to how science informs public policy. A PET scan carries a small but real radiation dose; it is justified when the benefit (detecting a life-threatening tumour) outweighs the risk. But the same dose from an unnecessary scan would not be justified.

Nuclear power stations generate electricity without producing carbon dioxide during operation, which is a significant benefit in the context of climate change. The risks include the possibility of accidents (though serious accidents are rare), the generation of long-lived radioactive waste, and the security concerns around nuclear materials. Societies make decisions about nuclear power by weighing these factors — there is no purely 'scientific' answer because the weighting of values (environmental, economic, security) is a matter of policy, not just evidence.

Radioactive waste is classified according to its activity and how long it remains dangerous:

• High-level waste — the most radioactive, typically spent fuel rods from nuclear reactors. Generates significant heat from ongoing decay. Must be stored securely for very long periods — thousands of years — because the isotopes involved have long half-lives. Current approaches include vitrification (encasing in glass) and storage in deep geological repositories.
• Low-level waste — items such as contaminated protective clothing, gloves and tools used in hospitals and nuclear facilities. Activity is relatively low and can be safely compacted and stored in near-surface disposal facilities.

The challenge of long-term storage is significant: no human institution has yet existed for the thousands of years that high-level waste remains dangerous. This is one of the key ethical arguments raised by those who oppose nuclear energy expansion.

Safety Precautions

Workers who handle radioactive sources follow strict precautions to minimise their radiation dose:

• Minimise time — spend as little time near the source as possible.
• Maximise distance — radiation intensity decreases rapidly with distance from the source.
• Use shielding — lead-lined containers, lead aprons and concrete walls absorb radiation.
• Use tongs — never handle sources directly; long tongs increase distance and prevent contamination.
• Monitor exposure — workers wear film badges or dosimeters that record their cumulative radiation dose so that legal dose limits are not exceeded.
• Wear protective equipment — gloves and lab coats prevent radioactive material contaminating the skin.

Key Fact

All uses of radioactive materials require risk–benefit analysis. Benefits include medical diagnosis, cancer treatment and low-carbon electricity. Risks include radiation exposure, contamination and long-lived radioactive waste requiring secure storage for very long time periods.

The best answers acknowledge that reasonable people can disagree depending on how they weight different values. For contamination vs irradiation, be precise: contamination involves the source being on or in the body; irradiation is external exposure only.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Contamination involves radioactive material deposited on or inside the body — ongoing exposure that cannot be stopped by moving away. Irradiation is external exposure that stops when the source is removed.
  • Medical uses of radiation include tracers (gamma, short half-life), PET scans (positron emitters) and radiotherapy (gamma/beta targeting tumours).
  • Risk–benefit reasoning is central to all decisions about radioactive materials — weighing evidence about benefits against evidence about risks, under conditions of uncertainty.
  • Nuclear waste ranges from high-level (requires secure storage for thousands of years) to low-level (near-surface disposal). Safety precautions minimise time, maximise distance, use shielding and monitor exposure.

lessons.title: Particles, Heating and the Particle Model
lessons.description: Internal energy, specific heat capacity, change of state, and the limits of the particle model.
lessons.content_html:
The Particle Model and States of Matter

The particle model explains the properties of solids, liquids and gases in terms of the arrangement and movement of particles. In a solid, particles are closely packed in a regular arrangement, vibrating about fixed positions — this explains why solids have a definite shape and volume. In a liquid, particles are close together but can move past each other — liquids have a definite volume but no fixed shape. In a gas, particles are widely spaced and move rapidly and randomly in all directions — gases have neither a fixed shape nor a fixed volume.

As a substance is heated, its particles gain energy and move faster (or vibrate more vigorously). Temperature is a measure of the average kinetic energy of the particles. The higher the temperature, the faster the average particle speed. This is why gases exert pressure — the constant collisions of particles with container walls create an outward force.

Key Fact

Temperature measures the average kinetic energy of particles. Internal energy is the total energy (kinetic + potential) of all the particles in the substance — it depends on both temperature and the amount of material.

Internal Energy and Specific Heat Capacity

Internal energy is the sum of the kinetic energy and potential energy of all particles in the system. When a substance is heated, energy is transferred into its internal energy store. This can either:

• Raise the temperature — particles move faster, increasing their average kinetic energy. The substance stays in the same state.
• Cause a change of state — particles gain potential energy to overcome attractions, and temperature stays constant during the change.

Different materials require different amounts of energy to raise their temperature by the same amount. This is captured by specific heat capacity (c). The equation is:

$$\Delta E = m \times c \times \Delta\theta$$

Where \(\Delta E\) is the change in thermal energy (J), \(m\) is mass (kg), \(c\) is specific heat capacity in J/(kg °C), and \(\Delta\theta\) is the temperature change in °C. Water has a high specific heat capacity (approximately 4 200 J/(kg °C)), which is why it is used in central heating systems — it can carry a large amount of thermal energy for its mass.

Question: A 2 kg block of aluminium (specific heat capacity 900 J/(kg °C)) is heated from 20 °C to 80 °C. Calculate the energy transferred.

Step 1: Temperature change: \(\Delta\theta = 80 - 20 = 60 \text{ °C}\)

Step 2: \(\Delta E = m \times c \times \Delta\theta = 2 \times 900 \times 60 = 108\,000 \text{ J}\)

Interpretation: This energy has been transferred from the heater's electrical energy store into the internal energy store of the aluminium block.

Changes of State and Specific Latent Heat

When a substance changes state (e.g. melts or boils), energy is transferred but the temperature does not change. The particles are gaining potential energy — not kinetic energy — to overcome the attractive forces holding them together. The energy required for a change of state is described by specific latent heat (L):

$$E = m \times L$$

Where \(E\) is energy in joules, \(m\) is mass in kg and \(L\) is specific latent heat in J/kg. There are two types: specific latent heat of fusion (melting/freezing) and specific latent heat of vaporisation (boiling/condensing). These values are much larger than those needed to raise temperature — it takes far more energy to evaporate water than to heat it from 0 °C to 100 °C.

The key changes of state are: melting (solid → liquid), freezing (liquid → solid), evaporation/boiling (liquid → gas), condensation (gas → liquid), and sublimation (solid directly to gas, as with dry ice). All changes of state are physical changes — they are reversible and no new substances are formed. Mass is always conserved.

Evaporation occurs at the surface of a liquid at any temperature — the fastest-moving particles at the surface have enough energy to escape as gas. Boiling occurs throughout the entire liquid at the specific boiling point. Evaporation causes cooling because the most energetic particles leave the liquid, reducing the average kinetic energy of the remaining particles. This is why sweating cools the skin — evaporation of sweat removes thermal energy from the body surface.

Limits of the Particle Model

The particle model is a very useful tool for explaining the behaviour of matter, but like all scientific models, it has limitations. The model treats particles as identical, hard, spherical objects with no size or internal structure. In reality, atoms and molecules have complex internal structures and interact through a range of forces. The model cannot fully explain phenomena such as surface tension, viscosity or the precise behaviour of real gases at very high pressures or very low temperatures. Recognising these limitations is part of good scientific thinking — models are tools, not perfect pictures of reality.

Key Fact

During a change of state, energy is transferred but temperature does not change. Specific latent heat describes this energy per kilogram. Specific heat capacity describes energy needed to change temperature without changing state.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For specific heat capacity calculations, always calculate the temperature change (ΔΘ = final − initial) before substituting — a very common error is to use the final temperature alone. For questions about heating curves, explain each section: rising lines = temperature increasing (kinetic energy increasing); flat sections = change of state (potential energy increasing, temperature constant). For 6-mark questions on the particle model, evaluate its strengths and limitations rather than just describing states of matter — this is what earns Mastering level marks.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The particle model explains states of matter through particle arrangement and motion. Temperature measures average kinetic energy; internal energy is the total kinetic + potential energy of all particles.
  • Specific heat capacity: ΔE = mcΔθ. The energy needed to raise temperature depends on mass, material and temperature change.
  • Specific latent heat: E = mL. Energy transferred during a change of state does not change temperature — it breaks or forms particle attractions.
  • All models have limitations. The particle model treats particles as identical hard spheres, which oversimplifies real atomic interactions.

lessons.title: Materials Under Stress and Density
lessons.description: Hooke's law, elastic vs plastic deformation, density, and why materials behave the way they do.
lessons.content_html:
Stretching and Deformation

When forces are applied to an object, they can change its shape. To stretch, bend or compress an object, at least two forces are needed — a single force would simply accelerate the object. When two opposing forces act on a spring (for example, a weight pulling it down while a support holds it up), the spring deforms. There are two types of deformation:

• Elastic deformation — the material returns to its original shape and size when the force is removed. The spring 'bounces back'.
• Plastic deformation — the material is permanently deformed. It has been stretched beyond its elastic limit and will not return to its original shape even when the force is removed.

Key Fact

Elastic deformation is reversible — the object returns to its original shape. Plastic deformation is permanent — the object remains deformed after the force is removed.

Hooke's Law

Hooke's Law states that the extension of a spring is directly proportional to the force applied, as long as the elastic limit is not exceeded. The equation is:

$$F = k \times e$$

Where \(F\) is force in newtons (N), \(k\) is the spring constant (N/m), and \(e\) is the extension in metres (m). Extension is the change in length — \(e = \text{stretched length} - \text{original length}\). A higher spring constant means a stiffer spring that is harder to stretch. The equation can be rearranged to find spring constant (\(k = F/e\)) or extension (\(e = F/k\)).

On a force–extension graph, Hooke's Law gives a straight line through the origin. The gradient of this straight line equals the spring constant \(k\). Beyond the elastic limit, the graph curves — the extension increases more rapidly for the same increase in force, and the spring undergoes plastic deformation.

Question: A spring has a spring constant of 250 N/m. A force of 15 N is applied. Calculate the extension, assuming the elastic limit is not exceeded.

Step 1: Rearrange: \(e = \frac{F}{k} = \frac{15}{250} = 0.06 \text{ m}\) (6 cm)

Check units: F in newtons, k in N/m, e in metres.

Now try: A spring extends by 0.04 m when a force of 20 N is applied. What is the spring constant? (Answer: \(k = 20/0.04 = 500 \text{ N/m}\))

A standard investigation hangs a spring from a fixed support and adds weights one at a time, recording the extension after each addition. Measure the original length of the spring before adding any load, then measure the length after each mass is added. Extension = current length − original length. Plot force (y-axis) against extension (x-axis) — a straight line through the origin confirms Hooke's Law is obeyed. The gradient gives the spring constant.

Safety note: do not overload the spring — once plastic deformation occurs, the spring cannot return to its original length and results will be unreliable. Use a clamp stand secured to the bench, and place a cushion or tray below the masses in case the spring snaps.

Density

Density is the mass per unit volume of a material. It tells you how much matter is packed into a given space. The equation is:

$$\rho = \frac{m}{V}$$

Where \(\rho\) (Greek letter rho) is density in kg/m³, \(m\) is mass in kg and \(V\) is volume in m³. In everyday calculations, g/cm³ is also used. To convert: 1 g/cm³ = 1 000 kg/m³.

Density explains why objects float or sink. An object floats in a fluid if its average density is less than the fluid's density. Ice (density approximately 0.92 g/cm³) floats on water (1.00 g/cm³) because it is less dense. Steel ships float because their overall average density — including the air inside the hull — is less than water.

The particle model explains density: denser materials have more mass packed into the same volume — either because their atoms are heavier, or because the atoms are packed more tightly. Solids are generally denser than liquids (they are more tightly packed), and liquids are denser than gases. Water is an exception — ice is less dense than liquid water because ice has a more open crystal lattice structure.

For a regular solid (cuboid, cylinder), calculate volume from dimensions and measure mass using a balance. For an irregular solid, use water displacement: partially fill a measuring cylinder with water and record the volume. Submerge the solid and record the new volume. The volume of the solid = new volume − original volume. Mass ÷ volume = density.

For a liquid, measure a known volume using a measuring cylinder, then measure the mass of the liquid alone (subtract the cylinder mass). Density = mass ÷ volume.

Key Fact

Hooke's Law: \(F = ke\). Spring constant = gradient of force–extension graph. Density: \(\rho = m/V\). Objects float when their average density is less than the surrounding fluid's density.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For Hooke's Law calculations, always check whether the question specifies the spring is 'within its elastic limit' — if not, you cannot assume Hooke's Law applies. When reading a force–extension graph, the spring constant is the gradient of the straight-line section only. For density questions, unit conversion is a common source of errors: check whether mass is in grams or kilograms, and volume is in cm³ or m³. For 6-mark extended questions on materials, evaluate the trade-offs (e.g. a very stiff spring needs a large force but gives a small extension — useful in some contexts, not others).
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Elastic deformation is reversible (spring returns to original shape); plastic deformation is permanent (spring stays stretched).
  • Hooke's Law: F = ke. Extension is proportional to force within the elastic limit. Spring constant k = gradient of force–extension graph.
  • Density: ρ = m/V. Denser materials have more mass per unit volume. Objects float when average density is less than the fluid's density.
  • The particle model explains density differences: more massive atoms, or more tightly packed atoms, give greater density.

practice_questions.text: A spring has a spring constant of 400 N/m. Calculate the force needed to extend it by 0.025 m, and state whether you would expect the spring to return to its original length when the force is removed, giving a reason.
practice_questions.marks: F = k × e = 400 × 0.025 = 10 N [1 mark]. Assuming this is within the elastic limit, the spring would return to its original length because the deformation is elastic (reversible) [1 mark].

practice_questions.text: Explain what a force–extension graph shows about a spring's behaviour within the elastic limit and beyond it.
practice_questions.marks: Within the elastic limit, force and extension are directly proportional, so the graph shows a straight line through the origin [1 mark]. The gradient of this line equals the spring constant [1 mark]. Beyond the elastic limit, the graph curves — extension increases more rapidly for each added unit of force, and the spring undergoes plastic (permanent) deformation [1 mark].

practice_questions.text: A stone has a mass of 180 g. When placed in a measuring cylinder containing 50 cm³ of water, the water level rises to 110 cm³. Calculate the density of the stone in g/cm³, and suggest what this tells you about whether the stone would sink or float in water.
practice_questions.marks: Volume of stone = 110 − 50 = 60 cm³ [1 mark]. Density = 180 ÷ 60 = 3 g/cm³ [1 mark]. Water has density 1 g/cm³; the stone (3 g/cm³) is denser than water [1 mark], so the stone would sink — objects sink when their density exceeds that of the fluid they are placed in [1 mark].

practice_questions.text: Engineers designing springs for car suspensions need to choose a spring constant that is high enough to support the car's weight without excessive compression, but not so high that the ride is uncomfortably stiff. Evaluate the factors they should consider when selecting an appropriate spring constant, and explain how Hooke's Law is used in this design process.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (5–6): Hooke's Law (F = ke) tells engineers how much the spring will compress under a given load — they can calculate the expected compression for the car's mass. A higher spring constant gives less compression (stiffer ride); a lower spring constant gives more compression but a smoother ride. The spring must operate within its elastic limit at all expected loads — if it reaches its elastic limit, deformation becomes permanent and the spring fails. Factors to evaluate: total mass of the vehicle including passengers and cargo (determines the load); road surface conditions (bumps cause additional transient forces); materials — different spring materials have different spring constants and elastic limits; cost and weight of spring (heavier springs affect fuel efficiency). Engineers may use different springs for front and rear axles depending on load distribution. Conclusion: spring constant selection is a trade-off between ride comfort and sufficient load support; both Hooke's Law calculation and testing within the elastic limit are essential. Secure (3–4): Correct Hooke's Law application and two relevant factors. Developing (1–2): States what spring constant is without applying it to the context.

practice_questions.text: Explain, using the particle model, why ice floats on water despite being made of the same molecules.
practice_questions.marks: Ice has a regular open crystal lattice structure in which water molecules are arranged with more space between them than in liquid water [1 mark]. This means ice has a lower mass per unit volume (lower density) than liquid water [1 mark]. Since ice is less dense than the water beneath it, it floats — objects float when their density is less than the fluid they are in [1 mark].

glossary_terms.definition: Deformation that is reversible — the object returns to its original shape and size when the deforming force is removed.
Deformation that is permanent — the object does not return to its original shape when the deforming force is removed.
The extension of a spring is directly proportional to the applied force, provided the elastic limit is not exceeded.
A measure of the stiffness of a spring — the force per unit extension. Measured in N/m. A higher spring constant means a stiffer spring.
The maximum force that can be applied to a spring before it permanently deforms. Beyond this point, Hooke's Law no longer applies.
The mass per unit volume of a substance. Measured in kg/m³ or g/cm³. Density = mass ÷ volume.
